sites.name: Blue Hole
sites.description: Dahab's most famous dive site and one of the most recognizable in the world -- a near-circular sinkhole in the reef table roughly 100m across that drops past 100m before opening onto the open sea floor beyond. Recreational dives and snorkelers stick to the shallow reef rim and the six-metre-deep Saddle at its seaward edge, whose ledge is thick with coral and reef fish; the Arch, a 26m tunnel through the wall at 55m connecting the hole to open water, is a technical dive only and has no place in a recreational dive plan.
sites.pro_tip: The Blue Hole has a well-documented history of diver fatalities, almost all from divers attempting the Arch beyond their training or without a proper gas plan -- reputable Dahab operators won't take anyone to the Arch without a verified technical certification (commonly Tech 60 or equivalent) and a trimix plan. Stick to the Saddle and rim for a completely safe, spectacular recreational dive or snorkel.

sites.name: El Bells
sites.description: A dramatic drift that begins at a narrow vertical crack in the reef table -- the 'bell' shape that gives the site its name -- descending through a chimney to around 26-28m before opening onto a sheer coral wall that drifts south into the Blue Hole, forming Dahab's classic 'Bells to Blue Hole' dive. Entry is a one-diver-at-a-time squeeze through the crack, and the wall beyond drops well past recreational limits, so depth discipline matters from the first kick.
sites.pro_tip: Time your entry for a lull between groups -- the chimney only fits one diver at a time, and it's easy to end up queuing on the surface if you arrive as another center's group is descending.

sites.name: The Canyon
sites.description: A narrow, dramatic fissure in the reef -- a separate site from Eilat's Canyon of the same name -- reached across a shallow sandy lagoon before a garden of hard and soft coral gives way to a split in the reef table that plunges from about 23m to over 50m. Usually combined with the nearby Blue Hole on the same trip, the Canyon's cracks and swim-throughs are shrouded in glassfish and occasionally hide octopus in the walls.
sites.pro_tip: Ask about the full-moon night dive here -- it's a well-known local specialty and a very different experience from the daytime coral-garden approach.

sites.name: The Islands
sites.description: Three coral formations linked by mazy coral corridors in El Qura Bay, reached by wading across a wide, shallow reef platform that's only comfortably crossed at high tide. Navigation among the coral heads takes some getting used to with multiple route options through the maze, but the payoff is one of Dahab's most photogenic reefscapes, along with regular sightings of blackfin barracuda schools and blue-spotted rays tucked under the coral.
sites.pro_tip: Cross the entry platform on a rising tide, not a falling one -- attempting it at low tide means dragging gear over exposed reef, and it's the single most common complaint about an otherwise excellent site.

sites.name: Lighthouse
sites.description: Dahab's original reef and its busiest dive and snorkel site, right in the middle of Masbat Bay with an easy sandy shore entry used by everyone from first-timers to instructors running courses. Large coral pinnacles close to the surface shelter Napoleon fish, moray eels, turtles and the occasional seahorse or ghost pipefish, and a shallow saddle behind the pinnacles opens onto a coral garden thick with table corals and gorgonians -- also one of Dahab's best pure snorkeling spots, not just a dive site.
sites.pro_tip: Check behind and beneath the reef statues and buoyancy-training platform near the entry -- seahorses and ghost pipefish turn up there more reliably than out on the open pinnacles, though both take a sharp eye since they vanish into the background at a glance.

sites.name: Eel Garden
sites.description: Dahab's own eel garden -- a distinct colony from the ones in both Sharm el Sheikh and Eilat -- reached across a reef plate to a canyon at about 9m that opens onto a broad sandy slope where garden eels sway in the current. Thick schools of barracuda regularly patrol the open sand beyond the eel colony, and the site is also one of the more reliable places in Dahab to spot the rare seagrass ghost pipefish.
sites.pro_tip: Dive it early morning or late afternoon when the light rakes low across the sand -- it's both when the barracuda schools are most active and when the garden eels stay up longest instead of retreating at midday.

sites.name: Napoleon Reef
sites.description: A large coral tower rising from a sandy seabed around 20m in Dahab's Laguna, reached by boat or zodiac about 450m offshore and named for the Napoleon wrasse that patrol it -- a reliable, easy site that boat trips also use as a snorkeling drop-off on the shallow reef tip. Eagle rays, large stingrays, turtles and moray eels round out the sightings alongside the resident Napoleon fish.

sites.name: Gabr El Bint
sites.description: The southernmost and most remote of Dahab's named sites, roughly 20km down the coast toward Ras Mohammed and reachable only by boat, 4x4 or camel; its isolation has left the reef in excellent condition. Two distinct dive areas here -- a coral garden and drop-off, and a separate crack-and-canyon system with a small 'baby Blue Hole' -- are framed by huge gorgonian fan corals, with the main drop-off continuing well past recreational depths.
sites.pro_tip: Ask specifically for the Shabb Sayed side with the giant gorgonian fans if your boat only plans to dive one of Gabr El Bint's two areas -- it's the more scenic and less-visited half of an already lightly-dived site.

sites.name: Ras Abu Galum
sites.description: A Bedouin-protected nature reserve about 13-15km up the coast from Dahab, reached by boat or an early-morning camel trek, with more than a dozen individual dive sites strung along a pristine, rarely-dived stretch of reef. Turtles and eagle rays are seen reliably along the coral gardens and pinnacles, and it's one of the few spots near Dahab with credible, if occasional, hammerhead, oceanic whitetip and manta ray sightings.
sites.pro_tip: Go as an overnight camel safari rather than a day boat trip if you can -- the Bedouin camp dinner and stargazing are part of what makes Ras Abu Galum worth the extra effort, and it lets you dive the reserve at dawn before any other boats arrive.

sites.name: Three Pools
sites.description: Three natural sandy pools in the reef plate, each only 3-4m deep and linked by coral saddles, forming an easy entry and exit south of Moray Garden; from the third pool a sandy alley lined with brain, pipe and salad coral leads down to the dive's deepest point around 27-30m before a coral garden with a resident turtle. A young Napoleon fish is often seen loitering near the third pool before the descent.
sites.pro_tip: Start on a high tide -- moving between the three pools over the connecting coral saddles is noticeably easier with more water over them, and low tide can leave you scraping over exposed coral to get from one pool to the next.

sites.name: Mashraba
sites.description: An easy-to-overlook reef at the southern end of Dahab bay that regularly outperforms its reputation, built around a prominent coral bommie known locally as Roman's Rock. Heading south from the rock brings you past a series of striking coral formations to a stand of large table corals around 20m, with a glassfish- and anthias-covered pinnacle to finish the dive in the shallows.

species.description: A master of disguise that drifts head-down among seagrass and soft coral, its elongated snout and mottled brown-green colouring making it nearly indistinguishable from a swaying blade of seagrass -- hence its local nickname 'seagrass ghost pipefish'. Usually found in male-female pairs, with the larger female brooding eggs in a pouch formed by her pelvic fins.
species.habitat: Seagrass and soft coral, head-down among fronds
species.population_info: Least Concern and widely distributed across the Red Sea and Indo-Pacific, but its slow-swaying seagrass mimicry makes it one of the hardest reef animals to actually spot despite being genuinely present.

species.description: A long, eel-like pipefish with a bent, double-tapered body that lies motionless among seagrass and sand, relying on its brownish, faintly spotted camouflage rather than speed to avoid notice -- a favorite subject for Dahab's macro photographers, particularly in the sandy shallows at the start of the Canyon dive.
species.habitat: Seagrass, sand and rubble near reef edges
species.population_info: Least Concern and found throughout the Indo-Pacific and Red Sea; poorly documented population trend, but not considered threatened.
